title: How to Implement Cookie Authentication in ASP.NET Core
description: Implement cookie-based authentication in ASP.NET Core without Identity.

data.text: **Cookie Authentication** in ASP.NET Core lets you implement custom authentication logic without using ASP.NET Core Identity at all. It is useful when you need lightweight, cookie-based sign-in for a simple site or an API frontend.

terms.definition: A string identifier for a registered authentication handler. CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme is the standard cookie scheme name.
The URL unauthenticated users are redirected to when they access a protected resource.
Represents the authenticated user. Wraps one or more ClaimsIdentity objects and is serialized into the auth cookie.
Extension methods on HttpContext that create or delete the authentication cookie.

data.text: There are three steps to use cookie authentication: (1) register the cookie scheme in Program.cs, (2) call UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() in the middleware pipeline, and (3) apply [Authorize] on controllers or actions that need protection.

data.title: Program.cs — register cookie authentication
Middleware Order Matters
data.text: UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() MUST be placed between UseRouting() and the endpoint mapping call. Swapping the order will cause unexpected behavior.
Any controller or action decorated with [Authorize] will only respond to authenticated users. Unauthenticated requests are automatically redirected to the LoginPath configured above.

data.title: SecuredController.cs

data.text: In a real app you would validate credentials against a database. Here we keep it simple with a hard-coded check. On success we build a ClaimsPrincipal and call SignInAsync(), which writes the cookie to the browser.

data.title: HomeController.cs — Login POST action

data.text: You can control how long the cookie lives by setting options in AddCookie. Sliding expiration resets the timer on each request, keeping active users signed in.

data.title: Program.cs — cookie options

data.caption: Cookie authentication request lifecycle
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant Server
    participant CookieStore
    Browser->>Server: GET /Secured (no cookie)
    Server-->>Browser: 302 Redirect to /Home/Login
    Browser->>Server: POST /Home/Login {user, pass}
    Server->>Server: Validate credentials
    Server->>CookieStore: SignInAsync — write .AspNetCore.Cookies
    Server-->>Browser: 302 Redirect to /Secured
    Browser->>Server: GET /Secured (with cookie)
    Server->>Server: Authenticate via cookie
    Server-->>Browser: 200 OK — Secured page

data.text: When an unauthenticated user requests a protected URL, ASP.NET Core stores the original URL and appends it as a ReturnUrl query string to the login redirect. After a successful login, redirect the user back to that URL.

data.title: Returning the user to the originally requested page
Exercise: Add Cookie Auth to a New App
data.description: Create a fresh ASP.NET Core MVC project and implement cookie-based sign-in from scratch.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core MVC project.
Register cookie authentication in Program.cs with a 15-minute expiry.
Add Login and Logout actions to HomeController.
Verify that accessing /Secured redirects to /Home/Login, and that login sets a cookie.
data.expectedOutcome: Visiting /Secured redirects unauthenticated users to the login page. After submitting valid credentials, the user is redirected back to /Secured with a cookie set.

items.text: UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() between UseRouting() and MapControllerRoute()
[Authorize] applied to controller or action that needs protection
SignInAsync called after successful credential validation
SignOutAsync called on logout to remove the cookie

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Cookie authentication works without ASP.NET Core Identity.
ClaimsPrincipal + ClaimsIdentity represent the authenticated user inside the cookie.
Sliding expiration keeps active users signed in without manual re-login.
data.takeaway: Cookie auth is the foundation that Identity builds on. Next, see how Identity adds user management on top.
